This paper presents Agent S, an open framework for desktop GUI automation with multimodal LLMs. The core proposal combines three ingredients: hierarchical manager/worker planning, retrieval from external web knowledge plus two internal memories (narrative memory for task-level summaries and episodic memory for subtask-level trajectories), and an Agent-Computer Interface that exposes a language-centric observation/action abstraction over screenshots and accessibility trees. On OSWorld, the paper reports a substantial improvement over the cited baseline, from 11.21% to 20.58% success rate with GPT-4o, and also shows gains on WindowsAgentArena without explicit adaptation.

Overall, I find the paper timely and practically relevant. GUI agents are an important emerging area, and the paper addresses several real bottlenecks: long-horizon planning, grounding in dynamic interfaces, and adaptation to application-specific knowledge. The empirical gains on OSWorld are meaningful, and the paper is generally well motivated. The framework is also modular and intuitively sensible. In particular, the distinction between task-level and subtask-level memory is a useful design choice, and the ACI argument—that MLLM agents benefit from a bounded, language-level action interface with immediate feedback—is compelling.

That said, I have mixed feelings about the degree of scientific novelty and the strength of the evidence supporting some of the claims. Much of the system is an integration of now-familiar agent design patterns: hierarchical planning, retrieval augmentation, reflection, memory, OCR-enhanced grounding, and constrained action spaces. The paper’s contribution is therefore primarily at the systems level. That is acceptable for an applied agent paper, but then the burden is on the evaluation to isolate which design choices matter, how robust the gains are, and whether the method generalizes beyond the exact benchmark setup. The current experiments partially support this, but not fully.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the main benchmark result. A jump from 11.21% to 20.58% on OSWorld is large in relative terms, and the per-category improvements, especially on Daily and Professional tasks, are encouraging. The cross-OS transfer result on WindowsAgentArena is also a positive sign that the framework is not narrowly overfit to Ubuntu. The ablations on web knowledge, narrative memory, and episodic memory are directionally useful and suggest that all three help. The error analysis is also appreciated; it is good to see the authors acknowledge that execution and grounding remain major failure modes.

However, there are several weaknesses that limit my confidence in the conclusions.

First, the evaluation methodology around memory construction raises concerns about possible benchmark contamination or task leakage. The initial memory is built through “self-supervised exploration” using tasks generated from applications used in OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena, and for environment-aware tasks the method explicitly uses the initial environments of tasks in OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena to generate different tasks. This is potentially problematic. Even if the generated tasks are nominally different from the benchmark tasks, using benchmark initial states to construct memory may leak substantial information about the test distribution and interface configurations. Since the method’s central claim is learning from experience, it is crucial to disentangle genuine generalization from benchmark-specific pre-exposure. The paper does not provide enough detail to assess this risk. How many exploration tasks are generated? Are any benchmark task templates, websites, documents, or application states reused? Are memories built separately per benchmark, or jointly? Are test tasks ever used for continual memory updates before evaluation on later tasks? This matters a lot.

Second, the continual memory update during inference complicates the interpretation of reported results. The paper states that the agent “continues to learn even during inference” and updates memory as it encounters new tasks. If evaluation is performed sequentially with memory carried across tasks, then the reported benchmark score is not a pure per-task zero-shot or fixed-policy evaluation. It becomes an online learning setting, and task ordering may matter. That is not inherently invalid, but it must be made explicit and compared fairly against baselines under the same protocol. The paper currently does not clearly specify whether OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena results are obtained with frozen memory, with online updates, or both; nor whether task order is randomized and averaged. This is a major reproducibility and fairness issue.

Third, the comparisons are somewhat narrow. The main baseline appears to be the OSWorld agent under the same input setting, which is reasonable, but the paper would be much stronger if it compared against stronger memory/planning baselines such as exemplar-based prompting or retrieval-augmented planning methods adapted to OSWorld. Since the proposed method is largely a composition of known ingredients, the key question is whether this particular composition is better than simpler alternatives. For example, how much of the gain comes from just replacing coordinate actions with element-ID actions? How much comes from OCR augmentation alone? How much comes from hierarchical decomposition versus simply prompting a single agent with retrieved task exemplars? The paper gestures at some of this, but the evidence is incomplete.

Fourth, the ablation section is useful but not yet rigorous enough. The ablations are run on a 65-task subset rather than the full benchmark, which is understandable for cost reasons, but the subset is small and category counts are tiny in places, especially OS with only 6 tasks and Professional with 10. This makes several percentage differences unstable. No confidence intervals, standard errors, or repeated-run statistics are reported, despite the stochasticity of LLM agents and retrieval pipelines. Some reported numbers also appear overly precise given the sample sizes, for example 24.49% on a 16-example category. More broadly, the paper should report variance across multiple runs or at least across multiple task orderings if continual memory update is enabled.

Fifth, some of the claimed novelty is overstated. The “textual rewards” framing is evocative, but in practice the self-evaluator is summarizing trajectories into memory entries rather than providing a reward signal in the reinforcement learning sense. Likewise, the analogy to hierarchical reinforcement learning seems more metaphorical than technical. I would encourage the authors to tone down these claims and present the method more plainly as retrieval-based self-improvement with hierarchical decomposition. That would make the paper more precise.

Sixth, the ACI contribution is promising but under-specified in important details. The paper argues that the ACI improves grounding and safety by using screenshots plus an image-augmented accessibility tree and a bounded primitive action space. This is plausible, but the exact action vocabulary, observation formatting, and grounding resolution are relegated to the appendix. Since ACI is one of the main contributions, the main paper should more concretely specify what actions are available, how element IDs are assigned and updated across time, how OCR boxes are merged with accessibility nodes, and what happens when the accessibility tree is incomplete or stale. The error analysis suggests grounding remains a major bottleneck, so these details are central rather than peripheral.

Seventh, the paper does not sufficiently discuss computational cost. The method uses a manager, workers, retrieval from web and memory, OCR, reflection, and self-evaluation. This likely incurs substantial latency and API cost. Since the paper itself notes that wall-clock time and step count are unaddressed, the current evaluation leaves open whether the gains come at a practically prohibitive cost. Even a simple table with average steps per task, average number of model calls, and approximate token/API usage would significantly improve the paper.

There are also several smaller issues. The writing is generally understandable, but there are places where terminology is inconsistent or imprecise. The paper sometimes says Claude-3, sometimes Claude-3.5-Sonnet. The references contain a duplicate Autoguide citation labeled 2024a and 2024b with the same title and metadata. Figure numbering appears inconsistent in the text around Figures 6 and 7. The qualitative example shown is too limited to be informative; a richer end-to-end example with retrieved memory snippets, generated subtasks, and recovery from an error would better illustrate the method. Finally, the paper mentions poor performance on the “Task Automation Challenge” but does not explain this benchmark or analyze why performance is low.

My main suggestions for improvement are as follows. First, clarify the evaluation protocol in detail: whether memory is frozen or updated during benchmark evaluation, whether task order matters, whether results are averaged over multiple orders, and whether exploration uses any benchmark-derived states or tasks. Ideally, report both a frozen-memory setting and an online continual-learning setting. Second, strengthen the ablations with repeated runs and uncertainty estimates, and if possible evaluate key ablations on the full benchmark or a larger subset. Third, add stronger baselines that isolate the value of each major ingredient: ACI only, retrieval only, hierarchical planning only, and a simpler exemplar-prompting baseline. Fourth, provide a more careful leakage analysis for the self-supervised exploration phase, especially when using benchmark initial environments. Fifth, include efficiency metrics and perhaps a success-versus-cost tradeoff analysis. Sixth, sharpen the claims of novelty and avoid RL analogies unless they are technically justified.

In terms of significance, I think the paper is valuable as an engineering contribution to GUI agents. The benchmark gains are real and likely useful to the community, especially given the open-source release. But from a top-tier ML conference perspective, the paper currently feels more like a strong systems integration with promising empirical results than a fully convincing scientific advance. The main risk is that some of the reported gains may depend on evaluation choices around memory construction and online updating that are not yet sufficiently controlled.

My recommendation is borderline positive but not unequivocal. If the authors can convincingly address the evaluation protocol concerns, especially around memory leakage and online adaptation during testing, the paper would become substantially stronger. As it stands, I view it as an interesting and practically impactful paper with meaningful results, but with important methodological ambiguities that should be resolved before strong acceptance confidence.

If I were to summarize succinctly: the paper tackles an important problem, proposes a sensible and modular framework, and achieves impressive benchmark improvements, but it needs clearer experimental controls, stronger isolation of contributions, and more transparency about memory construction and evaluation dynamics.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper presents Agent S, an open framework for desktop GUI automation with multimodal LLMs. The system combines three main ideas: (1) experience-augmented hierarchical planning, where a manager retrieves web knowledge and narrative memory to decompose tasks into subtasks and workers retrieve episodic memory for execution; (2) continual self-updating narrative and episodic memories built from self-supervised exploration and inference-time experience; and (3) an Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) that uses screenshots plus an augmented accessibility tree and constrains actions to language-level GUI primitives. On OSWorld, the paper reports an improvement from 11.21% to 20.58% success rate over a GPT-4o baseline, and also reports gains on WindowsAgentArena without explicit adaptation. The paper includes ablations over memory, web knowledge, ACI, and hierarchical planning, as well as an error analysis.
strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: general-purpose GUI agents for real desktop environments.
The overall system design is intuitive and modular, combining planning, retrieval, memory, and interface abstraction in a coherent framework.
The proposed ACI is a practically meaningful contribution: accessibility-tree grounding plus constrained primitive actions is a sensible design for GUI agents.
Empirical gains on OSWorld are substantial in absolute terms relative to the reported baseline, and the paper evaluates on the full OSWorld test set rather than only a tiny subset.
The paper includes several ablations and an error analysis, which helps identify where gains may come from and where failures remain.
Cross-benchmark evaluation on WindowsAgentArena is useful evidence that the framework is not entirely benchmark-specific.
The paper is clearly motivated and generally well written, with a strong systems perspective and open-source intent.
weaknesses: The main empirical improvements are demonstrated against relatively limited baselines rather than against the strongest contemporary agent frameworks under carefully matched conditions.

The contribution is largely an integration of known ingredients—retrieval augmentation, hierarchical planning, memory, accessibility-tree grounding, OCR augmentation, and constrained actions—so the novelty of each individual component is moderate.

The evaluation lacks statistical rigor: there are no confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run variance estimates despite likely stochasticity from LLM inference and environment interaction.
The ablation study is conducted on a small sampled subset of 65 tasks, which may be too small for stable conclusions across heterogeneous task categories.

The memory construction and continual update protocol raises concerns about evaluation contamination or benchmark adaptation, but the paper does not fully clarify safeguards against leakage from test-task interaction into future test performance.
The self-evaluator is central to the method, yet its accuracy and failure modes are not quantitatively validated; erroneous self-labeling could corrupt memory.

Claims around 'learning' and analogy to hierarchical reinforcement learning are overstated, since the method is primarily retrieval-augmented prompting with self-generated summaries rather than optimization of a policy or value function.
The paper acknowledges low absolute performance (20.58% on OSWorld, 12.5% on Task Automation Challenge), which limits practical impact despite relative gains.
methodological_flaws: Potential evaluation leakage/confounding: the agent performs continual memory updates during inference and may learn from benchmark tasks as evaluation proceeds. Unless evaluation is strictly single-pass with no reuse of information across test tasks, reported gains may partly reflect test-set adaptation rather than pure generalization. The paper does not specify enough protocol detail to rule this out.

The initial memory is built using environment-aware tasks derived from OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena initial environments. This may inadvertently encode benchmark-specific priors and reduce the strength of generalization claims, especially if exploration tasks are generated from benchmark states closely related to evaluation tasks.

The comparison on WindowsAgentArena is not fully apples-to-apples: the baseline and Agent S differ not only in planning/memory but also in action interface assumptions and possibly model/tooling details. The fairness claim is therefore only partial.

The paper makes strong causal claims from ablations, but the ablations are run on a small, stratified subset with very small per-category counts (e.g., OS has 6 tasks), making category-level conclusions statistically fragile.
No repeated trials are reported. Given nondeterminism in GPT-4o/Claude outputs and GUI interaction, single-run success rates may be noisy; this weakens confidence in both main results and ablations.

The formalism in Section 3 is descriptive rather than analytical; there are no mathematical guarantees or proofs, which is acceptable for a systems paper, but the text occasionally overstates rigor by invoking hierarchical reinforcement learning despite lacking corresponding objective functions, update rules, or theoretical grounding.

The self-evaluator uses no human feedback or ground truth, yet its summaries are treated as reliable rewards/memory entries. Without validation of evaluator precision/recall, the memory update mechanism may propagate systematic errors, and the paper does not quantify this risk.

The error analysis categories are subjective and may overlap substantially; because a single task can contain multiple errors, the reported percentages are difficult to interpret causally and do not isolate bottlenecks cleanly.
